text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Kristoff Memo, Minister of
State, Head of Government of the
Principality of Monaco.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
President of the General Assembly,
Secretary General,
heads of state, heads of government,
delegates, your excellencies, ladies and
gentlemen,
I am addressing you as the
representative of the smallest member
state of this organization in terms of
its land mass and one of the smallest in
terms of its population, barely two
squared kilometers bordering the
Mediterranean.
And yet in this forum
there are no small or large states. Here
every one of the 193 members has a
voice,
one alone and of the same weight. Here
the charter only recognizes states equal
in sovereignty, equal in rights but also
and I wish to stress this point equal in
terms of responsibility
because the equality that our
organization beso bestows upon us is not
a privilege that we enjoy. It is a
responsibility that we bear. This
responsibility is our shared unique duty
to uphold the law and multilateralism.
Shared because no state, regardless of
how powerful it is, can preserve peace
alone or address global threats alone.
Unique because
everybody must shoulder it without
leaving it to others to honor the
promise of San Francisco.
It is this message that his serene
highness prince Albert II, the prince of
Monaco, charged me with bringing to this
rostrm with his greetings of trust and
friendship.
President, the Principality of Monaco
wishes sincerely to congratulate you
upon your election to the presidency of
this 81st session,
for which you have chosen the topic
restoring trust, managing
transformation,
a UN that delivers for all. You can
count on the full support of my country.
And I also wish to warmly thank the
Secretary General Antonio Gutterz who is
finishing his second mandate amidst
particularly grave circumstances.
Why does a state such as mine believe so
strongly in international law? The
answer goes for all. When might makes
right, it is the smallest states who are
the first to be threatened. When force
is regulated by the law, all of humanity
is protected. Sovereign equality between
states, honoring commitments, peacefully
settling disputes are therefore not
abstract concepts. They are our front
line of protection and yours too with
the balance as is set out by the charter
between the three pillars peace and
security development and human rights.
Nevertheless, this protection is today
under assault.
Rearmament is accelerating throughout
the world. We are seeing the use of
force once again as being another
political tool for some. Trade is
breaking down and we're seeing a race to
capture critical resources.
The private sector is also part of this
of these power relations. We are now in
the era of the geoeconomy and this is
fertile ground for disinformation which
undermines people's trust in their
institutions and leads them to question
verifiable facts. Our belief has never
been tried to such an extent since 1945.
In Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, the
Sahel, in many other places out of the
media spotlight, civilians are paying
the price for conflicts which have
discarded the most basic rules of
humanity.
And never since 1945 has the very
legitimacy of states and multilateral
bodies such as the UN being called into
question to such an extent.
Given this danger, let us recall our
mission. In the words of Dam Damsky, the
second secretary general of the UN, the
UN was not created to take mankind to
heaven, but to save humanity from hell.
That is the exact scope of our task. And
that is why we do not have the right to
give up. First, in Ukraine, for almost 5
years, a permanent member of the
Security Council has been waging a war
of aggression against the sovereign
state in flagrant violation of the
charter.
From the very outset, Monaco condemned
this aggression
unambiguously and unreservedly.
We voted in favor of all of the general
assembly's resolutions calling and
demanding for Russian forces to
withdraw. We took all restrictive
measures aligned with EU measures. And
we also provided our humanitarian
supports to the Ukrainian people and
hosted people displaced by the war.
Our support is unwavering and it will
remain so. Monaco will never recognize
any annexation of territory obtained
through force.
Allowing this for one state would be t
tantamount to allowing it for all. The
principality welcomes the ongoing
diplomatic efforts and hopes that they
will lead to fair, comprehensive,
lasting peace, respecting Ukraine's
sovereignty and territorial integrity.
next to the Middle East. Monaco was
greatly relieved by the ceasefire which
entered into force in Gaza and the fact
that the hostages were freed. Nothing
can ever justify the acts of terror of
the 7th of October, but nor can anything
justify the price paid by these
civilians in Gaza. The principality
calls on all parties to strengthen the
fragile ceasefire and to respect every
stage of it, ensuring full, safe,
unhindered humanitarian access.
We support efforts to rebuild Gaza and
we are concerned about the ongoing
violence in the West Bank in the
occupied territories
which ride roughshod over human rights
and dishonor democratic values.
Our our belief remains the same. The
only viable option is the two-state
solution. Israel and Palestine
living side by side in peace and
security.
within safe and recognized borders. Any
policy that makes that scenario less
likely through settlement building or
sewing terror makes peace less likely
too. In Lebanon too, Monaco supports
deescalation efforts and calls on all
parties to fulfill their commitments.
First and foremost, Security Council
resolution 1701.
The people of Lebanon Lebanon have the
right to a fully sovereign state in
peace throughout its territory.
In the Persian Gulf, finally, tensions
around Iran remain a source of deep
concern. Monaco pays tribute to all the
civilian victims of the conflict and
reiterates its solidarity with the
countries of the Gulf who have been
affected by the attacks.
Here again, only negotiations can lead
to a global agreement on the Iranian
nuclear program and will prevent further
escalation. Above and beyond these
crises, Monaco will continue to
contribute to international cooperation.
focused on the least developed countries
through its support to the International
Committee for the Red Cross, the High
Commissioner for Refugees, and the World
Food Program
through development aid geared towards
the health, education, and empowerment
of women and girls.
Restoring trust also means changing the
organization itself.
Monaco supports the UN80 initiative to
make the organization more streamlined,
more understandable, more efficient, and
closer to people on the ground. Still,
the UN needs resources to function. My
country fulfills its financial
contributions in full and on time, and
we call on all other states to do
likewise.
But this necessary step is not enough in
the light of the changes that have to be
undertaken. That is why Monaco calls on
the real leaders of the United Nations
to rethink the architecture of our
system from 2030. Bringing on board the
public and private sector, civil society
and educational and cultural hubs.
Streamlining processes, preventing
mandate duplication, consolidating
specialized agencies, regional centers
and the secretariat, and guaranteeing
small states genuine inclusivity. There
is plenty of work to do. The time of the
law is patient, but this patience should
not be confused with inertia.
In the same vein, the principality is in
favor of a reform of the security
council to make it more representative
to today's realities
while also preserving its ability to
act.
And we're also in favor of the
revitalization of this general assembly,
the House of Equality between states.
This session will also see the election
of the next secretary general of the
organization. Monaco calls for a
transparent, inclusive, and rigorous
process. After 80 years, the
principality hopes that women candidates
will be seriously considered.
The organization would do well to
demonstrate at its helm the equality for
which it stands.
Ladies and gentlemen, there is one area
where multilateral trust has recently
produced tangible results and it is dear
to the heart of his serene highness
Prince Albert II and that is to say the
ocean. The entry into force of the
agreement on marine biodiversity of
areas beyond national jurisdiction which
Monaco was one of the first countries to
sign and ratify is a victory of the law
over seizure, of cooperation over
predation.
We now need to translate these
commitments into acts to protect 30% of
the ocean by 2030 to finally agree on an
ambitious and binding agreement on
plastics pollution and exercise extreme
caution with regards to deep seabed
mining.
The ocean is nobody's property.
It is everyone's responsibility. Monaco
will continue to do its part in this
vital task, relying on science, which is
the only universal compass.
And what goes for the ocean also goes
for the climate. The Paris agreement
remains our common framework. Monaco
will honor its commitments by reducing
greenhouse gas emissions by 67.5% by
and by achieving carbon neutrality by
2050. The principality calls on all
countries to show more ambition in their
national contributions and not to
abandon
island and coastal states which are the
most vulnerable.
Because the climate crisis is no longer
a distant threat. Heat waves, fires, and
floods are multiplying. And the
Mediterranean, which my country borders,
experienced last year its second highest
surface temperature ever recorded.
And because science is being questioned,
let us recall, as the prince did in COP
30 in BM, that science has never been as
certain, as accessible, and as clear.
Four years before the 2030 deadline, the
sustainable development agenda must not
become the symbol of our broken
promises.
Let us be candid as we take stock.
States alone cannot make progress.
We need to have a renewed framework for
cooperation with those who create wealth
and shape innovation, businesses first
and foremost and civil society.
Lastly, preparing for the future and
ensuring it benefits everyone means
mastering technological changes.
Artificial intelligence is creating
enormous opportunities for human
development, but it also entails genuine
risks. The global dialogue on AI
governance, which was held this year in
Geneva, confirmed this. These
technologies must remain at the service
of humanity and the United Nations
cannot remain a spectator.
Monaco supports the implementation of
the global dig digital compact and a new
normative framework on AI
based on law and shared ethical
principles respecting human rights and
being accessible to all states.
Finally, the principality calls for
strengthened cooperation to deal with
cyber threats and for inclusive
transitions
both within states and within societies.

Prize in literature. The great French
writer Alber Camus defined the task of
his generation thus not to reform the

but perhaps even greater
to prevent the world from destroying

Today that is our task preventing the
world from destroying itself. preventing
law being destroy destroyed by force,
preventing trust being destroyed by
mistrust, and preventing the planet from
being destroyed under the weight of our
negligence.
Trust is not decreed. It is won through
deeds and through promises kept.
That is the overarching principle that a
state such as mine aims to fulfill.
being consistent, keeping our word.
Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of his
serene highness, Prince Albert II, I
wish to reiterate the commitment of
Monaco to the United Nations, to its
charter, and to the ideal that led to
its establishment, saving future
generations from the scourge of war, and
building together a common house where
even the smallest states can take their
rightful place, because here the law
protects them all. This pledge will only
be fulfilled through the might of the
law and not through might makes right.
Thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the Minister of State, head of
government of the Principality of
Monaco.
